source.title: SuperValid: Capability-Aligned OOD Validation for Generalizable Downstream Scaling
source.authors: Quan Sun; Chang-Xin Tian; Kensen Shi; Cai Chen; Cun-Yin Peng; Jia Liu; Kun-Long Chen; Zhi-Qiang Zhang; Jun Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling of a capability-aligned OOD validation loss and whether validation loss predicts downstream capability, using a different loss construction and fitting method from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on SuperValid loss, IID and weighted IID loss, and downstream capability prediction. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded. Prompts in the appendix instruct models used for data synthesis; they are not instructions to an AI reviewing the paper.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own results on whether validation loss predicts downstream capability (V6). It finds ordinary IID validation loss fails across architectures, data mixtures and a mid-training data switch, while its synthesized OOD loss succeeds. That is a result that V6 needs restating. A small from-scratch MoE sweep also shows log-linear scaling of its OOD loss (V1).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude IID validation loss is an unreliable proxy for downstream capability, especially under distribution shifts and across model scales. SuperValid loss correlates strongly and stably with domain capability across architectures, scales and data changes, and obeys a log-linear scaling law, supporting model selection, early stopping and scaling decisions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthesized capability-aligned OOD validation set and sigmoid fits to benchmark-aggregated domain capability, rather than the original studies' pretraining-loss scaling measurements and compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss-to-capability prediction varies with validation construction: domain-level loss outperforms single-benchmark loss; full knowledge extraction and expansion improve prediction over blank filling or retrieved text. IID loss is sensitive to a mid-training data-mixture switch, whereas SuperValid loss is reported as robust.

fits_no_version.finding: How the validation set is constructed changes how well loss predicts capability. Knowledge-domain MSE is 7.29e-3 for blank filling, 2.31e-3 for retrieved text and 6.73e-4 for the full pipeline. Domain-level sets beat single-benchmark sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The predictiveness of validation loss for downstream capability depends on validation-set construction; capability-aligned, diverse synthetic OOD text predicts better than benchmark-surface or raw retrieved text.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The model-scale sweep covers a limited stated range and tests SuperValid OOD loss rather than conventional IID pretraining loss. The study's domain capability targets are unweighted averages of benchmark scores, and the validation data are seeded from those benchmark collections. The authors note that native tokenizers may affect cross-family per-token loss comparability, validation-set size was not optimized, and only six domains were studied. Some numerical results are available only in figures whose values are not unambiguously recoverable from the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for per-domain Figure 3 or Figure 6 plotted values, because the text does not give numerical mappings from values to domains and methods. Figure 4 pointwise losses and Figure 7 transition gaps are also not stated numerically; their explicitly described aggregate outcomes are recorded in r1 and r14-r15.

untested.parts: Conventional IID held-out pretraining loss; token/data scaling with model size held fixed; ranges spanning several orders of magnitude; fitted exponents (none reported).
Entire version: no extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
Entire version: no fixed-compute allocation analysis.
Entire version: no controlled shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Entire version: no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Direct prediction of downstream performance from scale or compute. Prediction to larger, held-out models (fits are in-sample sigmoids). Domains beyond the six studied.
Entire version: no exponent or compute-optimal-split comparisons across fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-domain MSE values for IID, weighted IID and SuperValid loss. The flattened text lists values (e.g. SuperValid near 1e-4, IID near 1e-2) but they are unmapped; needed to quantify how far IID loss fails.
Per-domain MSE for the open-source-model sigmoid fits behind the 1.51e-3 average

record.verdict_notes: Tranche set to T5 rather than T2: the V6-relevant result is that ordinary loss-to-downstream prediction breaks under data and architecture changes. The reader's 'challenges' label on r15 is downgraded to limits_scope, because within-stage fits still hold. Rows r6–r7 and r11–r13 compare variants of the study's own method and are unlinked. Caveats: capability targets are averages of the same benchmarks that seed the validation data; cross-family losses use native tokenizers; sigmoid fits are in-sample, with no held-out extrapolation; V1 evidence is figure-only over about 1.5 orders of magnitude, with a learning rate that varies with scale.

versions.untested_parts: The scaling sweep uses SuperValid OOD validation loss, not a conventional IID held-out pretraining loss. It tests model scale and compute, not token-count scaling with other quantities varied independently. The reported parameter ranges are narrower than several orders of magnitude.
No test of fitting power laws on small runs and predicting runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute comparison of parameter/token allocations or test of compute-optimal parameter and token growth.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as instances of the same power-law form.

Tests SuperValid validation loss as a predictor of downstream benchmark-derived capability; it does not establish a general relation to pretraining loss or downstream task performance beyond the studied models, benchmarks, and domains.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, and no test of curves bending away from a single power law.
